---
title: "Why the second slice never tastes as good"
description: "The first bite of anything is the best one you will get. Economists have a dull name for this and a surprisingly useful lesson inside it."
image: /assets/social/why-the-second-slice-never-tastes-as-good-og.png
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-09-02"
categories: [behavioural economics, everyday]
---

Think about the last time you were really hungry and the first slice of pizza
arrived. That slice was perfect. The second was good. By the fourth you were
eating because it was there.

Economists call this diminishing marginal utility, which is a terrible name for
one of the most useful ideas you will ever learn. Each extra unit of something
gives you a bit less than the one before.

Once you see it, it is everywhere. The first coffee of the day is a small
miracle. The third is a habit. The first week of holiday is bliss. Week three
you are checking email. A pay rise feels enormous for two months and then
becomes the new normal.

Here is the practical part. Because the first unit of anything gives you the
most, you get more total pleasure by spreading things out than by piling them
up. One great meal a week beats three average ones. A short holiday twice a year
usually beats one long one. Small, frequent, and separated wins.

It also explains why the richest people you know do not seem proportionally
happier. The hundredth thousand does far less than the first.

The next time you are about to reach for the fourth slice, ask what the fourth
slice is really giving you. Often the honest answer is: not the pizza.
